cfi.summary: Possessing or growing cannabis for personal use is a minor offence under the Criminal Code, punished with a short arrest and a fine of €500–1,200. No medical programme.

First-offence penalties were softened in 2022, but personal use remains one of the world's strictest regimes, with trace amounts enough and mandatory deportation for foreigners from 1 January 2026. A separate 2026 law allows licensed industrial hemp and authorised hemp-derived medical products.

Cannabis is banned, and the Taliban's 2026 Penal Code for Courts sets fixed terms of six months to seven years for use, possession, cultivation and trafficking. There is no death penalty for cannabis in the code, but courts also impose flogging.
Adults may hold up to 15 g and a household may grow four plants; Rastafari sacramental use is recognised. Dispensaries serve patients only.
Licensed medical production is for export, with a separate industrial permit scheme. A small personal dose is exempt from the possession offence; unlicensed growing and supply carry prison terms.

Small possession and use are administrative offences with heavy fines, raised sharply in May 2026; sale and larger-scale growing are criminal. Industrial hemp is licensed at 0.3% THC, while psychoactive cannabis has no medical route.
Holding or using cannabis (liamba) for personal use is a crime with up to three months in prison, or up to a year above three days' supply; a court can suspend the sentence for treatment.
The Supreme Court's Arriola ruling (2009) protects private personal use. The REPROCANN registry lets patients grow their own or use a designated grower.

People caught with cannabis for personal use can have their case dropped after probation and any required health measures. Growing to obtain the drug is a crime. Patients can receive cannabinoid medicines, including dronabinol.

In the ACT an adult is outside the local small-possession and one-or-two-plant offences, within the limits ACT Policing states. Elsewhere, infringement notices, expiation fees, cautions and diversion are used for small amounts, and charges remain available. Medical cannabis is available on prescription. Presence-based drug-driving laws are strict.

Since 31 January 2020 an adult in the ACT is outside the local offence for a small quantity and for one or two plants. ACT Policing states the amounts as 50 g dried or 150 g fresh, and two plants per person, four per household. Selling and gifting remain offences.
Police may caution an eligible adult for up to 30 g of dried cannabis, at most twice. Possession remains an offence, with up to 20 penalty units or two years.

An adult may be given an infringement notice for less than 50 g of cannabis plant material, or for not more than two cannabis plants. The prescribed amount is 2 penalty units. A prosecution remains available if no notice is given.
An eligible person must be offered diversion for not more than 50 g of cannabis, at most three times. Possession remains an offence.
Small amounts are an expiation notice: $250 for less than 25 g of cannabis and $400 for 25 g to 100 g. One non-hydroponic plant is $400.
Police may caution for up to 50 g, up to three times in ten years; otherwise it is a criminal offence.
A small quantity on a first offence usually draws a caution if the person agrees to counselling. Up to 50 g is a fine; more than 50 g and under 250 g can bring a year.
Police may issue one Cannabis Intervention Requirement to an adult found with not more than 10 g. Possession remains a criminal offence.

Cannabis possession remains an offence, but the revised 2025 prosecution instruction provides for surrender and dismissal in the 0–30 g band, with exceptions. Larger personal amounts can attract fine requests. Low-THC CBD has a separate medicinal import route.

Small amounts for personal use are administrative offences, but a court can order up to two months' arrest; possession above 5 g, sale and cultivation are crimes. There is no medical, hemp or legal supply route, and the authorities report thousands of drug cases a year.

Illegal. In the Federation, unauthorized possession of a narcotic drug is a criminal offence with up to one year in prison, including for personal use. Republika Srpska's criminal code does not copy that offence. A December 2025 decision opened the way to cannabis-based medicines, but the prescribing rules it depends on will not be adopted in the Federation before 2027.
Up to 14 g is a fixable fine; a medical industry is licensed and Rastafari sacramental use is permitted.

Herbal cannabis carries six months to five years for up to 5 kg and up to ten years above 15 kg. A separate digital offence in the amendment dated 16 July 2026 can be punished with any term of imprisonment or death.
For adults, up to 3 g or one plant is the lowest prosecution priority — usually a simple police record. Medical access is confined to a few pharmaceutical products.

Cannabis use is criminalised and drug users face jail. The 2018 Penal Code set shorter prison ranges for small personal possession and growing, alongside fines. Parliament adopted a further replacement code on 20 October 2026.
A high-risk drug: ordinary possession carries one to six years and a fine. Minor cases carry a fine up to €511.29; qualifying first offenders can receive administrative release.
Personal possession and growing are crimes; trafficking can bring death or life imprisonment.
Cannabis possession and use are crimes; judges can impose one to five years in prison, a fine, or both.
Illegal for all purposes; possession is reported to carry two to five years in prison, with some informal tolerance outside the cities.

Simple possession of seven grams of cannabis or less has been decriminalised since 20 December 2017, while police may seize it and unauthorised use, growing and supply remain offences. Qualifying old convictions can be cleared on application. Named cannabinoid medicines have been permitted on prescription since 2014; the UK blocked the broader cannabis licensing bill in 2022.

Severe penalties include prison and, for specified trafficking offences, caning or a mandatory death sentence. Death sentences are imposed but no execution is known since 1957. Simple possession and consumption carry up to ten years; cultivation three to twenty years.

Recreational cannabis remains prohibited. A medically assessed personal-use quantity leads to compulsory treatment; possession above it falls under trafficking, with ten to twenty-five years in prison plus a fine. An individual compassionate medical import was reported in 2021, and a wider medical-access bill is pending in 2026.
In 2024 the Supreme Court decriminalised possession of up to 40 g or six female plants, now an administrative matter. Medical products are sold in pharmacies; policing remains uneven.
Cannabis remains criminal. The 2024 Act created a Cannabis Authority, but its possession, medical-use and licensing provisions have not been brought into force.

Cannabis grows wild across the country but possession is a criminal offence: up to 50 g of herbal cannabis is a misdemeanour carrying one to under three years, and larger amounts or trafficking reach five to under nine years. A treatment route covers up to twice the threshold in limited cases.

Possession of 60 g or less remains an offence, but a December 2025 amendment excludes prison and caps the fine at P10,000. Licensed medical and industrial cannabis is permitted, though no patient-dispensing route was verified.
Personal possession can bring short custody, restriction of liberty or two to five years in prison. A 2025 reform widened sentencing options; growing for drugs and recreational supply remain crimes.
Since 2017 adults may possess up to 10 g and use it on private premises. A regulated market law was shelved.
Fully legal since October 2018: 30 g in public, four plants per household in most provinces, gifting between adults, and licensed retail and delivery across the country.
Minimum age 18, the lowest Health Canada lists. Private licensed shops, in person and online. Use is allowed at a single-family home and where the municipality allows it.
Age 19. Government shops and private licensed shops. Adults may generally smoke or vape where tobacco smoking is allowed, with further bans in parks, near schools and in vehicles.
Age 19. Private shops. Since 1 May 2025 up to four plants may be grown indoors, locked or out of a young person's reach. Smoking and vaping in public are prohibited.
Age 19. Cannabis NB shops, approved private retailers and farmgate outlets. Adults may consume at a private dwelling, on its land, or at an occupied campsite.
Age 19. Government and private licensed shops. Adults may consume in a private dwelling or the yard attached to it.
Age 19. Sold only through the Nova Scotia Liquor Corporation. Combustible cannabis in public follows the Smoke-free Places Act, and a municipality may restrict it further.
Age 19. Approved vendors, including private shops, and online sales. A community may vote to restrict or prohibit cannabis.

Age 19. A person may possess up to 150 g of dried cannabis, and 30 g in public. Private licensed shops and online sales. Smoking cannabis is prohibited in publicly funded housing, including staff housing.
Age 19. Private licensed shops and a government online store. Smoking and vaping are allowed in many outdoor public places, and not in enclosed public places.

Age 19. Government-run shops only. Up to four plants, with a locked outdoor enclosure and written landlord permission for a tenant. Consumption is limited to a private home and its yard, or vacant land with the owner's consent.

Age 21. Home cultivation is prohibited. A private residence is limited to 150 g of dried cannabis. Smoking and vaping are prohibited in places open to the public. Retail sales are only through the SQDC.
Age 19. Private licensed shops, in person and online. Consuming cannabis in a public place is prohibited.
Age 19. Private shops supplied by the territorial corporation. Adults may consume at a private residence and its adjoining property, or at a registered campsite.
Recreational cannabis is prohibited. A 2022 ministerial order specifies licensing and controls for medical and scientific cannabis activities; an operating patient programme was not verified.
Cannabis is prohibited. The 2001 drug law distinguishes small personal possession and growing from ordinary production and trafficking, with a fine alone possible for small personal quantities.
The 2025 law allows a fine alone for small personal possession, purchase or growing; cannabis derivatives other than oil carry a one-to-six-month prison range.

Possessing up to 10 g for personal use is not punishable. Adult consumption can bring a CHF 100 fixed fine. Registered residents can buy regulated cannabis through scientific trials, and doctors can prescribe medical cannabis without a special federal permit.

Possession for personal use carries one to three months with treatment as the default response; supply and cultivation carry five to ten years. A licensing regime for medical cannabis does not operate.

Private personal use is not punishable and courts accept personal cultivation as a defence. Public use is a minor offence. A 2026 law could let trafficking penalties reach small amounts once its list of substances is written.

Growing cannabis is banned. The main offences allow 10 to 20 years in prison, a fine, or both; a small amount possessed, bought or grown for personal use falls under a lighter tier, and a court can waive punishment after a promise not to reoffend.
Use brings administrative detention and possible compulsory rehabilitation; trafficking can carry the death penalty. China is nonetheless a leading industrial hemp producer.
The 'personal dose' of 20 g and up to 20 plants are protected by constitutional case law. A licensed medical industry exists; adult-use market bills have repeatedly fallen short.
Personal possession is not penalised, and courts require evidence of trafficking before punishing home cultivation. A 2022 law legalised medical cannabis and hemp.
Simple cannabis possession can bring six months to two years, a fine or both. Cultivation carries four to ten years; aggravated drug offences can carry life imprisonment or death.

Small personal-use possession, cultivation and consumption are criminal but have a separate three-month-or-fine provision. Trafficking has heavier penalties. Scientific growing and controlled-medicine authorisations exist in law; a functioning cannabis patient service remains unverified.

Cannabis possession, use, growing and supply remain prohibited. Prosecutors’ guidance calls for confiscation and dismissal in the 0–25 g band, subject to exceptions, and a fine request in the 25–50 g band. The law provides medical exemptions for authorised professionals and lawfully obtained treatment supplies. A proposed medical-cannabis industry was still awaiting parliamentary approval in April 2023.

Cannabis possession and home growing remain crimes. Young first offenders have a two-year prison cap for personal-use offences; medical oil has a restricted approval-and-prescription route, alongside licensed hemp and medical-production laws.

Since 1 January 2026 adults aged 21+ may grow three plants and keep 100 g of cannabis at home or 25 g elsewhere. Recreational sales remain illegal. Pharmacies dispense medical cannabis on electronic prescription, with insurance covering 90% of the cost up to 30 g a month.

Since April 2024 any adult may carry 25 g. People who have lived in Germany for six months may keep 50 g at home, grow three plants and join a non-profit growing association. There are no shops, but medical cannabis is easy to obtain through pharmacies.
Illicit use carries up to one year and possession up to ten under the Penal Code; general sentencing rules let courts impose just one of the listed penalties.
Possession is punished with fines. The medical cannabis programme became permanent in 2026, and Denmark hosts licensed producers. Christiania's open market was shut down in 2024.
The 2020 reform exempts up to 28 g from ordinary possession penalties and permits three plants at a permanent home. School-premises possession can trigger a rebuttable trafficking presumption.

Personal possession of up to 20 g of marijuana can mean six months to two years in prison. An intent to distribute or sell can mean three to ten years at any amount, including below 20 g. More than one pound of marijuana attracts the trafficker tier of five to twenty years.

Personal use or possession carries two months to two years and a fine; personal growing two to five years. Supply and production carry ten years to life, and the 2025 law allows death for aggravated supply, never for simple use.
The constitution treats use as a health issue, though the possession threshold table was repealed in 2023. Medical cannabis and hemp are legal.

A small quantity for personal use is a misdemeanour, punished by a fine or detention. A large quantity, enough to intoxicate at least ten people, carries one to ten years. Medical access exists but is rarely used.
Hashish and bango are widely used, but the law is harsh: prison for possession, and large-scale trafficking can carry the death penalty.
Cannabis remains prohibited. Eritrea’s published 2015 drug penalties were still awaiting enforcement in the government’s 2024 account and a 2025 UN report.
Private use and cultivation out of public view are not crimes; possession or use in public brings fines from €601. Hundreds of cannabis social clubs operate in a legal grey zone.
Possession for personal use can bring up to seven years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of up to 50,000 Birr. Supply with the intent to traffic starts at five years.
Use itself is a criminal offence, typically fined. Medical cannabis is available to a small number of patients.

Cannabis possession remains criminalised, with court guidelines favouring non-custodial sentences for up to 100 g. A separate hemp exemption was approved in 2022. A drug-law rewrite signed in October 2026 provides for commencement by ministerial notice.

Cannabis penalties vary by state. The national code’s $50 small-possession provision is not a nationwide ceiling: published state laws also allow custody, and the available Chuuk drug-law appendix is historical.

Recreational possession and growing remain offences, including small personal quantities. Doctors have been able to prescribe medical cannabis through a trial scheme since April 2019. Patients receiving it are told not to drive.

One of Europe's strictest laws alongside its highest use rates. Since 20 August 2026 ordinary illicit use can be ended by a fixed fine of €500, or €400 if paid within 15 days and €1,000 if the fine is increased. A medical experiment has run since 2021. CBD flower is legal.
Cannabis is prohibited. The 2020 Penal Code separates illicit use, carrying up to one year and a fine, from general possession and direct supply, which carry longer prison terms.
A Class B drug; small amounts often end in a warning or community resolution. Medical cannabis is legal since 2018 but almost exclusively through private clinics.

Since February 2026 adults 21 and over may possess up to 56 g. Four plants at a household are outside the growing offence, and the agriculture ministry says a grower registers with the Cannabis Secretariat before planting. The ministry said the rules for signing up would follow. There is no legal shop yet. Smoking on school premises, or in public/open areas within 100 yards during school hours, can carry up to twenty years in prison.

Private cannabis consumption is legal, while possession, growing and sale remain restricted. Parliament restored prison for possessing more than 5 g of dried cannabis in July 2025. In June 2026 the Constitutional Court barred imprisonment in a case about 0.1315 g of personal-use resin under the pre-May-2025 code; criminal liability remained.

Recreational possession remains criminal, with fines common in small cases and much harsher treatment for imports. Medical cannabis is available privately. Certain CBD preparations have a retail exemption, with an age restriction applying from October 2026.

The 2020 Narcotics Control Commission Act fines possession for personal use. Buying a narcotic drug or plant for personal use is a separate offence, and the Second Schedule allows a fine of 2,000 to 10,000 penalty units or four to ten years in prison. A 2023 amendment licenses low-THC cultivation for industrial and medicinal purposes.

Cannabis possession and home growing are crimes, with fines or imprisonment available. Medical access is limited to controlled medicines: trained public-health doctors may authorise approved cannabis-based products for specified conditions, with smoking prohibited.

Recreational cannabis possession and supply remain prohibited. Greenland’s own rules provide medical and prescription permissions and an exception for products with no more than 0.2% THC brought in through authorised importers for local distribution. The government continues to emphasise customs controls, prevention and treatment.
First-time possession of 0.1–150 grams carries a 50,000–100,000-dalasi fine, one to two years in prison, or both.
Cannabis possession and use are offences. The 2016 Penal Code gives small personal possession, purchase and growing a separate one-to-three-year range, a value-based fine, or both.

Drug possession remains a serious offence. The 1993 decree expressly covered cultivation, possession, use and gifts; its penalties need reconciliation with the 2022 Penal Code. A report of open use in 2000 does not establish current tolerance.
Personal use is a misdemeanour that is rarely jailed. Medical cannabis was legalised in 2017 and production licences are issued.

Acquiring or possessing cannabis for personal consumption carries four months to two years in prison plus a fine. A reasonable amount for immediate use and the circumstances determine personal possession; the law gives no fixed gram allowance. Unauthorised growing and supply carry longer prison terms.

Adults 21 and over may hold limited amounts, give cannabis away and grow six plants per residence, with no more than three flowering. Medical patients have a separate home-growing permit. Commercial supply has faced years of delays: the first grower's operating permit was approved in June 2026, with retail still pending.

The 1993 decree-law criminalises use and small personal possession or cultivation, with different custody bands for high-risk plants, cannabis oil and other cannabis derivatives. Its youth waiver is conditional, not a general first-offender exemption.

Since 2022 possession of up to 30 g no longer carries prison, but counselling or community service. Section 6 provides death if unlawfully supplied narcotics cause the death of someone under eighteen.

Possession and use carry up to seven years in prison; very small first-offence personal-use cases may receive a fine, probation or community service. Growing cannabis carries up to fifteen years. CBD has also been controlled since February 2023.

Since 25 June 2020 the criminal code punishes cannabis trafficking, cultivation and possession for those purposes with four to seven years, or one to three when the case is of lesser gravity. The 1989 compulsory-rehabilitation rule for personal use was repealed. That repeal does not declare personal possession lawful.
Possession for personal use has been a misdemeanour since 2013. The penalty is a fine of €663.61 to €2,654.46, or up to 90 days' detention. Medical cannabis is prescribable since 2015.
Holding or growing a small amount for personal use carries up to six months and a fine under the 2001 drug law; trafficking carries up to thirty years.
Zero-tolerance policy, toughened further in 2025; diversion is available only for first-time small-quantity offenders.

Class I narcotic. Since 2 January 2026, possessing plant material is up to twelve years and possessing dried cannabis over 5 g can bring life or twenty years. Aggravated sale or production can still be death. Medical use is prohibited.
Since September 2026, eligible first-time possession cases can receive a health referral. The Medical Cannabis Access Programme covers only a few conditions.

Possession and use for personal consumption are administrative offences carrying a fixed fine, not a criminal record, but police issued no such fines between 2022 and 2025. Above 15 g the law presumes dealing unless the accused rebuts it; all growing and supply are criminal. Medical cannabis is legal and large: 145,758 active licences and prescriptions in June 2026.

Cannabis remains a Class B drug. Small possession cases can bring a fine or a drug-education referral; home growing remains criminal. Private medical dispensing expanded beyond a single-pharmacy pilot in 2024.

The NDPS Act bans flower and resin. Leaf-only bhang falls outside its cannabis definition, but state law differs: some states license shops, while Maharashtra restricts unauthorised possession and use. Some states license hemp and medical cultivation.

Personal use carries one to three years and a fine; trafficking can bring life imprisonment or death. The 2017 law has no quantity thresholds and divides use from dealing by intent. A first amendment was read in parliament in August 2026 but is not law.

Possession is punished with fines and lashes, and trafficking more than 5 kg of cannabis can carry death; 795 people were executed for drug offences in 2025. A 2017 amendment narrowed the capital threshold but did not stop the rise. Since October 2026 industrial hemp may be grown under permit, while medical cannabis still has no patient route.
Possession of small amounts is punished with a fine.

Personal possession brings administrative sanctions such as licence suspension. Courts have tolerated minimal home growing. Medical cannabis is legal since 2013; a 2025 decree banned the hemp-flower trade.

Cannabis is a Class B drug, but small amounts are usually settled at a Parish Hall enquiry with a written caution or a fine, neither of which appears on the person's criminal record. Private medical prescriptions are unusually common, and the island licenses medical cannabis growers. A decriminalisation debate was put off until after the 2026 election.
Since 2015 up to 2 oz is a petty offence with no record, five plants per household are allowed, and Rastafari sacramental use is legal. Licensed herb houses serve patients and visitors.

Cannabis remains criminal: personal plant possession can bring one to six months, a JOD200–500 fine, or both; resin carries one to three years plus a fine. First personal-use offences leave no criminal precedent or security record. Separate rules cover prescription CBD products and hemp seed foods.

Possession carries up to seven years, and since December 2024 use itself is a crime. The same reform allowed cannabis-derived medicines, though none has been approved yet; CBD is legal only within strict THC limits, and CBN was banned in June 2026.

Cannabis held solely for personal use carries up to five years or a fine of up to 100,000 shillings. Where that is not shown, 1 to 100 grams carries a fine of at least 30 million shillings, thirty years in prison, or both.

Small personal possession and small unauthorised cultivation are administrative offences. Larger amounts and supply remain criminal; the dried-marijuana table sets the small-quantity ceiling at 20 grams.

Cannabis is controlled under the 2012 drug law. Unlawful possession carries prison terms; the law retains limited discretion for customary consumption and cultivation and provides both voluntary and compulsory treatment procedures.
Cannabis possession, growing and gifts are offences; separate rules cover prescribed extracts and tinctures.
The 2021 Penal Code punishes holding, buying or using narcotics with 10 to 15 years in prison and production with 10 to 20 years. Cannabis was briefly legal here from 1975 to 1978.
A 2019 ruling protects adults' private personal use and growing. Later laws set ticket and licence rules; 56 g is the statutory ticket threshold, not the court's privacy test.

Legal status is opaque. Cannabis is listed as a narcotic and unauthorised storage or use is prohibited; hemp is widely grown. Scored with low confidence because no cannabis-specific penalty, prosecution or execution is published.

Up to five years for use, enforced even for use abroad by citizens. Sale carries at least a year, import or export life or at least five years, and profit-making or habitual import can bring death. A few cannabinoid medicines can be imported through a state agency.

Personal consumption or possession can bring up to five years, or ten in listed places. Unpaid sharing carries five to ten years. Trafficking, import, production or cultivation for trade can carry death or life; death is mandatory for listed aggravations.

Cannabis possession, use, growing and supply remain criminal offences. A doctor may prescribe extracts and tinctures through the medical route introduced in 2016. Voters backed decriminalising small amounts in April 2025; after a public consultation, the premier expected reform recommendations and supporting legislation in November or December 2026.

Unauthorized possession of even a small amount, without intent to sell, is a criminal offence under Article 296, with a fine, corrective work, community service or up to 40 days' arrest. An especially large amount can bring three to seven years. A proposal to take simple possession out of the Criminal Code has not been enacted. Wild cannabis covers the Chu valley.
Cannabis possession can lead to treatment or prison; licensed low-THC hemp medicines are permitted.

A 2020 law legalised licensed cultivation for medical and industrial use, but no licence had been issued by August 2026. Recreational use remains illegal: a small quantity for personal use brings three months to three years, while other possession or supply can bring life.
Adults have a 30 g possession exemption and may grow four plants per dwelling-house, subject to school-location restrictions. There is no legal market.

Personal possession, use and growing for one’s own consumption are criminal contraventions usually punishable by a fine. Cannabis-type narcotics at or above 1% THC are controlled; low-THC hemp and exceptional medical access have separate rules.
Illegal, but licensed Ayurvedic practitioners may dispense cannabis preparations. A separate export-only cultivation scheme began licensing foreign investors in 2025.
Cannabis use carries four months to one year on a first offence under the 2023 law. Possession and growing for personal use are separate felonies; trafficking is non-bailable.

First African country to license medical cannabis cultivation (2017), mostly for export. Personal use remains illegal although matekoane is widely grown. The 2008 Act has no standalone possession offence; prosecutors use its licensing and trafficking provisions.
Possession of any amount has been a criminal offence since 2017; decriminalisation has been repeatedly debated. Cannabinoid medicines are permitted.

Adults may grow four plants from seed per household and use their harvest at home. Small possession elsewhere can bring a €145 warning payment or a criminal fine. There is no legal recreational retail market.

The first-offence small-quantity tier depends on the product: up to 1 g dried cannabis, 5 g undried, 0.1 g hashish or 0.05 g resin/oil/extract. Above the relevant ceiling, or after a repeat warning, criminal penalties can apply.

Cannabis is banned in every form. Personal use or possession carries three to fifteen years; import, production or cultivation with intent to traffic carries death or life, and death is mandatory with aggravating facts.

Law 13-21 (2021) licenses cultivation for medical, cosmetic and industrial use in the Rif provinces. Recreational kif remains illegal but is widely tolerated; thousands of growers were pardoned in 2024.

Personal possession and use can bring six months to three years in prison or a fine. Group use, cultivation, supply and imports face higher statutory penalties; CBD retail products have also been prosecuted.
Small personal possession remains an administrative offence, with higher fines from August 2026. Supplying drugs carries prison terms; authorised industrial hemp has a separate route.

Personal drug possession carries a €100–€2,000 misdemeanour fine. Unlawful cannabis production, sale and giving cannabis to another person can bring prison; low-THC food and industrial hemp has a permit route.
Small personal quantities of cannabis bring two to six months, a fine, or both; rongony is nonetheless grown on a large scale. Cannabis is in Table I, with no medical, hemp or research route.
Cannabis offences carry fines or prison, with higher penalties for larger amounts and repeat convictions.

Since February 2023, the Criminal Code expressly excludes possession for personal use from punishment. Drug use still brings a separate misdemeanour fine, and unauthorised production and supply remain criminal. Licensed companies may grow for medical or scientific purposes; domestic patient access remains limited.

Cannabis is illegal. The 2001 law gives small personal supplies, including cultivation, a lighter penalty with a fine-only option. Ordinary high-risk drug cultivation carries five to ten years and a fine. A limited industrial-hemp authorisation was withdrawn in 2020.

Drug use itself carries no prison term. A user who does not enter the required treatment bond, or who breaks it, is sent to a rehabilitation centre for three months. Possession still carries multi-year minimum sentences, and more than 100 grams is deemed to be for sale.

Unauthorised acquisition or storage without a selling purpose can bring one to five years of travel restriction or imprisonment. Sale-related conduct carries two to eight years; organised criminal groups face twelve to twenty years or life.

Cannabis use, personal possession and home growing carry three months to a year in prison or a fine. Larger personal stocks can trigger production or trafficking penalties, including a lesser one-to-five-year tier. Medicines require official authorisation and controlled prescribing.

The Northern Mariana Islands legalised adult and medical use in September 2018. Adults 21 and over may carry an ounce, keep eight at home and grow their own. Licensed shops and lounges opened in 2021; in January 2026 the regulator moved from the Cannabis Commission to the Alcohol Beverage and Tobacco Control Division.

The 1993 law treats possession of any amount as high-risk trafficking: 15–30 years and a large fine, with death on a repeat conviction. Simple use can bring up to two years. Executions have been suspended since 1987.
First EU country to legalise (2021): 7 g in public, 50 g at home, four plants per household, and licensed non-profit associations. Public consumption remains prohibited.
Strict prohibition, but since 2022 medical cannabis can be approved by specialist committees in public hospitals.

Someone who is not drug-dependent is presumed to be dealing even with 5 g or less, and dealing is fifteen years. Use by a dependent person is three years. Trafficking is life, and bringing in more than 350 g of cannabis can be death.

The 2020 Cannabis Regulation Act legalised cultivation for medical and industrial use, including industrial hemp at up to 1% THC, under a licensing authority. Recreational use of the famous 'Malawi Gold' remains illegal.
The Supreme Court struck down the ban on personal use in 2021, but Congress never passed a regulatory law. Adults can seek a permit to grow and consume; there is no legal market.
Possession of 200 g or more is presumed trafficking, which can carry death (no longer mandatory since 2023). No cannabis medicine is registered for patients.
Use and personal possession carry up to two years plus a fine, with possible waivers for occasional users. More than three days' personal supply brings a one-year minimum.
Prohibited under a 1971 Act; over 115 g is presumed dealing. Court challenges by cannabis activists have failed so far.
Cannabis is a high-risk drug under the 1999 ordinance. Small personal possession and growing have shorter prison ranges, a fine, or both; a fine alone is expressly possible.

Cannabis possession carries long mandatory prison terms. Cultivation carries life under the NDLEA Act; the older Indian Hemp Act prescribes at least 21 years after its amendments. An October 2026 replacement bill remains before the Senate.
Under 5 g is a minor offence punished with day-fines and community service; 5 to 20 g brings up to three years in prison and more than that up to eight.
Formally illegal but tolerated: coffeeshops sell up to 5 g per person and five plants are usually only confiscated. A regulated supply-chain experiment now covers ten municipalities.
Possession is fined. After 2022 Supreme Court rulings, people with dependency are generally not punished for small amounts.
Illegal since 1976 but widely tolerated, notably during Maha Shivaratri. Legalisation bills resurface regularly.
Unlawful possession carries at least a year in custody; growing, supply and use face much longer prison terms.
Illegal, but since 2019 police must consider a health-based response before prosecuting. A legalisation referendum narrowly failed in 2020; the medical scheme has operated since.

Personal possession, use and growing carry one to three years and a fine, with treatment alternatives for established dependence. Unpaid supply carries seven to fifteen years; specified import and production offences for trade can bring death or life imprisonment.
Medical cannabis has a legal framework dating from 2021; licensed CBD sales began in 2026. Recreational cannabis remains illegal.

Ordinary immediate personal possession is exempt up to 8 g of marijuana or 2 g of derivatives. Registered medical patients and qualifying caregivers have a separate treatment-needs exemption. Medical cannabis and licensed patient-association cultivation are legal.

Cannabis, known locally as paka, is widely grown and banned. Cases go to the court in Papeete and usually end in fines. A 2023 medical cannabis law was repealed that November without ever being used. Its 2024 replacement allows low-THC hemp and cannabis medicines, and a pilot with nine growers is now under way.

Cannabis possession and cultivation are prohibited. The Controlled Substance Act has quantity tiers, including up to two years for 10 g or less and life for more than 2 kg or more than 20 plants. The Dangerous Drugs Act remains in force alongside it, carries a maximum of forty years and/or K1 million, and is still used for cannabis; the quantity tiers are not a guarantee of the only charge or penalty.

Possession carries prison at any amount. Life imprisonment can apply from 300 g of marijuana or 5 g of resin, and applies from 500 g or 10 g respectively. Unauthorised importation carries life regardless of quantity; possession at gatherings or with at least two others has enhanced penalties. Medical access requires an individual compassionate permit.

Illegal, yet charas is widely used and largely tolerated in parts of the country. The cannabis regulator publishes licence categories and application requirements for medicinal cultivation, extraction, manufacturing and industrial hemp.

Possession and home growing remain crimes, though small personal-possession cases can be dropped. Patients can obtain prescribed cannabis through pharmacies; prescribing normally requires an in-person examination. A proposal to exempt 15 g and one personal plant remains before parliament.

Unauthorised cannabis possession remains a felony, with probation and other alternatives available in qualifying cases. Medical dispensaries began serving patients in December 2016. The health department counted 110,736 active patients in August 2026.

The West Bank punishes personal use with six months to two years; trafficking reaches fifteen to twenty-five years. Gaza's 2013 law is harsher: three to fifteen years for use and death available for aggravated trafficking.

All drugs were decriminalised in 2001. Since 1 October 2023, 25 g of flower and 5 g of hashish are the ten-day reference amounts: proven personal possession stays an administrative matter for a dissuasion commission even above them, while a larger amount can still start a criminal inquiry. Cultivation remains a crime. Portugal is a major medical exporter.
Small possession is a $500 citation, not prison; giving away an ounce or less is treated the same. Cultivation and sale are felonies carrying up to eight years.

Up to 10 g exclusively for personal use may be exempt from punishment, subject to judicial assessment. A December 2025 medical THC/CBD pilot regulates specialist prescriptions and authorised dispensing; patient home growing remains prohibited.
Possession for personal use carries six months to three years and a fine. Non-residents are deported.

French prohibition applies: cannabis use, possession and growing are criminal offences, and the only patient route is the restricted national French medical framework. Locally the plant is known as zamal and grows wild in several regions.
Possession for personal use carries prison of three months to two years or a fine. Medical access is largely theoretical.

A small amount for personal use carries a fine or up to three years, with possible waiver or deferred prosecution. Cannabis growing carries two to eight years; a large stock carries three to ten years even when held for personal use.

The administrative tier is product-specific: up to 6 g of marijuana plant material, 2 g of hashish or 0.4 g of cannabis oil. Above the relevant threshold, criminal penalties apply. Drug propaganda is also penalised.

Cannabis sits in the highest drug category. Caught use or possession carries one to two years or community service; supply, transport, storage and production carry life imprisonment with a fine of more than 20 million and up to 30 million francs, subject to mitigation down to at least fifteen years. A licensing regime for medical cannabis exists but no patient supply was found.
Prison for possession and use; long terms or death for trafficking. Discretionary flogging ended in 2020, but drug executions resumed in 2022 and continued in hashish cases through 2026.

Cannabis possession, growing and gifting are offences. The published reprint gives up to six months on summary conviction or ten years on conviction with assessors, plus fines expressed in penalty units; current practice needs fuller verification.
CBD medicine rules introduced in 2020 require specialist assessment and public-health approval; recreational cannabis remains illegal.

Personal use and possession for use carry up to five years under the published narcotics statute. Unpaid supply carries at least ten years; aggravated trafficking can carry death. Current wartime enforcement remains insufficiently documented.
Zero-tolerance model: use itself is criminal and police can compel drug tests.

Death for trafficking more than 500 g of cannabis, more than 200 g of cannabis resin, or more than 1,000 g of cannabis mixture, with narrow exceptions. Larger possession amounts bring mandatory prison and caning. Ordinary consumption brings at least one year; qualifying repeat use can bring 13 years and caning. Registered cannabinoid medicines may be prescribed, and HSA may approve an unregistered one for a named patient.
Possession for personal use is a minor offence punished by a fine. Voters backed medical and personal use in 2024 referendums, and a 2025 law set up a full medical cannabis system.

Possession and personal growing remain crimes: even the lowest cannabis quantity band carries up to one year in prison, and up to two plants carries up to six months. Medical cannabis has no lawful access programme.
Cannabis possession and use remain crimes. The Pharmacy Board has rules for licensed medical cultivation and processing for export; patient access through local pharmacies has not been established.

Personal possession and use remain criminal, normally carrying six months to three years under the statutory scale, with a possible reduction for particularly minor personal cases. Medical cultivation and prescribing have separate authorisation rules.
Personal possession carries two months to one year in prison; trafficking ten to twenty years since 2007.
Cannabis remains prohibited; surviving drug laws prescribe prison, while enforcement depends on territorial control. Later amendments and nationwide sentencing practice remain incompletely verified.
Up to thirteen years for possession, with no Dutch-style tolerance. The 2023 industrial-hemp law provides licences for certified crops with no more than 1% THC.
Possession or use is up to five years, a fine, or both. Dealing is up to fourteen years, a fine, or both. The death or life sentence is written for a dangerous drug other than cannabis.

Cannabis use, possession and personal growing are crimes. The Penal Code allows a fine instead of prison for a small personal quantity, and courts may excuse an occasional consumer. Giving cannabis to another person falls under trafficking.
Article 34 sets prison for under 2 g, but since 2012 possession for one's own use is outside criminal punishment. Weight alone does not decide.

Cannabis possession remains an offence. Prosecutors can dismiss cases in the 0–25 g band after confiscation, subject to exceptions. The ordinance includes medical exemptions, while proposals for a regulated cannabis industry remain under debate.

Personal possession for use carries three to fifteen years and a fine, with a treatment route; smuggling, manufacture and cultivation carry death, and trafficking can bring death with aggravating facts. Captagon dominates enforcement.

Illegal, though "Swazi Gold" is a major smallholder cash crop. A 1922 Act and the 1929 Pharmacy Act both apply; the Pharmacy Act allows up to fifteen years for possession. Bills to license medical and hemp production have been debated for years but not enacted.

Chad prohibits cannabis. Its 2000 pharmacy law provides prison and fine alternatives for narcotics offences and compulsory treatment powers. The full 1995 drug law and a current consolidated account of the overlapping rules remain unverified, as do the scores below.
Cannabis remains illegal. The 2015 code sets one to three years for small personal-use amounts, a fine, or both; judges can substitute treatment for a person with drug dependence.

Flower has been a controlled herb since November 2022 and since June 2025 requires a prescription, which narrowed the dispensary boom to medical supply. From 2026 licences are limited to qualifying medical, pharmacy, herbal and cultivation premises with trained staff. Recreational use is officially no longer permitted.

Small possession and growing are administrative; from about 100 g of dried cannabis, 20 g of hashish or five plants they become criminal, with up to twelve years for possession or cultivation and twenty for supply.

Cannabis use, possession and growing solely for personal consumption carry up to one year or a fine; above 5 g of herb, 2.5 g of resin or 1.25 g of oil the ceiling is two years. Trafficking carries five to fifteen years. Courts may waive punishment for an occasional user.
Cannabis remains illegal. Small-amount possession and use can bring a fine or administrative detention; criminal possession carries up to five years.
Law 52 still makes use or possession of any amount a crime with one to five years, though since 2017 judges may go below the minimum. A full rewrite has been in committee since 2025.
Cannabis is a Class B drug. Under 28 g carries up to T$5,000 or a year in prison; 28 g or more carries up to T$50,000 or seven years. There is no medical, hemp or CBD exemption.
Possession carries two to five years, often converted to probation and treatment. Hemp is licensed in selected provinces; cannabinoid medicines have a tightly controlled individual import route.
Adults may ordinarily hold up to 30 g and grow four plants, but possession around children at specified premises or on school buses can bring five years in prison. There is no legal market.
A 2025 amendment sets minimum prison terms for small cannabis offences and permits medical or scientific licences; ordinary recreational supply remains prohibited.
Category 2 narcotic: up to three years for use; growing for personal use carries one to seven years since 2022, other cultivation at least five.

Mainland Tanzania provides at least thirty years for unlawful cannabis cultivation. A separate small-personal-use tier allows a fine, prison or both; trafficking penalties can reach life imprisonment.
Possession of up to 5 g is an administrative offence. Medical cannabis became legal in August 2024; the first patients received prescribed capsules on 11 June 2026.
Possession carries up to twenty years with no lesser tier for personal use; a handful of licences exist for medical cultivation for export.

Adult-use cannabis is still federally illegal, yet about half the states run licensed markets and 40 allow medical use; in April 2026 state-licensed medical cannabis was moved to Schedule III. Scores are a national estimate — reality ranges from retail shops to prison depending on the state.
Adults 21+ may carry 1 oz and grow six plants (three mature), keeping their full lawful harvest where it was grown. Licensed shops since 2016; some offer on-site consumption.

Possession for personal use is a misdemeanour with up to a year in jail; a second offence is a felony. Licensed medical sales to registered Alabama patients began on 4 June 2026. Raw flower and products that could be smoked or vaped are prohibited.
Under 4 oz is ordinarily a misdemeanour. With four qualifying prior possession convictions, 1–4 oz is a felony. Medical dispensaries serve card holders.
Adults 21+ may carry 1 oz total, including at most 5 g of concentrate, and grow six plants each, twelve per household. Licensed shops since 2021.
28.5 g of flower (8 g of concentrate) and six plants per household. Shops, delivery and licensed consumption lounges; many cities still ban sales.

Up to 2 oz may be possessed. A person 21 or older may give up to 1 oz, with no payment, to another person 21 or older. Six plants per adult, three flowering, in an enclosed locked space, and no more than 12 at a residence. Licensed shops since 2014; hospitality venues in some cities.
1.5 oz on you and 5 oz locked at home. Cannabis grown lawfully at the grower's own home does not count toward those limits. Six plants (three mature), twelve per household. Licensed shops since 2023.

2 oz may be possessed, and a person 21 or older may give up to 1 oz, with no payment, to another person 21 or older. Growing is up to six plants, three mature, inside the principal residence, and the household may not exceed 12 plants, six of them mature. Congress blocks licensed adult-use sales, so access runs through self-certified medical dispensaries.
Adults 21+ may hold 1 oz leaf marijuana, 12 g concentrate or products with 750 mg delta-9-THC. Shops opened in 2025; growing at home remains a crime.

Up to 20 g of flower is a misdemeanour; unauthorised resin or concentrates can be a felony at any weight. A large medical programme operates; a 2024 legalisation measure won 56% but needed 60%, and a 2026 attempt did not reach the ballot.

1 oz or less is a misdemeanour with up to a year in jail, though Atlanta and several cities have cut it to a small fine. From 1 July 2026 a registered patient may buy medical cannabis products, including flower for vaporization. Smoking it remains illegal.
Up to 3 g of marijuana plant material is a $130 violation. Concentrates have separate criminal penalties, including felonies from ⅛ oz. Card holders have a medical programme.
A first offence carries up to six months in jail. A narrow medical programme caps THC per patient.
No medical programme and no decriminalisation: under 3 oz is a misdemeanour with up to a year in jail and a mandatory minimum fine.
Residents 21+ may hold 60 g of flower, visitors 30 g. Only medical patients may grow (five plants); for others a few plants is a $200 civil fine. Licensed shops since 2020.
Possession ordinarily carries up to 180 days. Prior drug convictions and separate marijuana/hash thresholds can make it a felony. No medical programme.
No medical programme. A first possession offence is a misdemeanour with up to six months in jail; a second qualifying offence carries up to a year, and a third is a drug severity level 5 felony.

Up to 8 oz is a misdemeanour capped at 45 days in jail. A medical programme began in 2025; smoking flower is not allowed under it. By 12 October 2026, dispensaries operated in all eleven licensing regions.
Outside enhanced school zones, up to 14 g carries at most a $100 fine with no jail. Medical cannabis, including flower, is sold through licensed pharmacies.

Since April 2026, adults may hold 2 oz of flower or the Commission-defined product equivalent (10 oz plus lawful homegrown harvest at home); six plants per adult, twelve per household. Licensed shops since 2018, but a November 2026 ballot question would end recreational sales.

Adults 21+ may hold 1.5 oz flower, 12 g concentrate or products with 750 mg delta-9-THC. An ordinary household may grow two plants; qualifying medical patients 21+ may grow four. Licensed shops since July 2023.
Adults 21+ may carry 2.5 oz total, including at most 10 g of concentrate, and grow six mature plants, twelve immature plants and unlimited seedlings. Licensed shops since 2020.

Adults 21+ may carry 2.5 oz, keep 10 oz at home plus the harvest of up to twelve plants lawfully grown there, and buy from licensed shops. Cannabis above 2.5 oz at home must be secured with locks or other functioning security devices.
Adults 21+ may hold 2 oz of flower in public or 2 lb at home, 8 g concentrate, and a combined 800 mg THC in edibles. Eight plants (four mature); licensed shops operate.
3 oz is legal. Registered growers 21+ may keep six flowering plants, six larger non-flowering plants and six clones. Licensed shops since 2023.

Ordinary first possession of up to 30 g brings a $100–250 fine. A driver with more than 1 g in the passenger area can face up to 90 days in jail, even on a first offence. Medical dispensaries serve cardholders.

Adults 21+ may hold one ounce equivalent: 1 oz flower, 8 g concentrate or 800 mg THC in products, with combinations counted together. The regulator limits home growing to Montana residents. Shops operate only in counties that voted for legalisation.

The ordinary no-active-jail tier covers up to ½ oz of marijuana plant material or 1/20 oz of hashish. Larger resin quantities and isolated THC can be felonies. No state medical programme; Cherokee tribal law is separate.
Under ½ oz marijuana is a criminal infraction; THC uses separate 2 g and 6 g thresholds. Adult 21+ ingestion is not itself an offence under the ingestion statute. Medical cannabis is available.
A first offence with up to 1 oz is a $300 infraction. Voters approved medical cannabis in 2024; the regulated supply chain remains unfinished as of October 2026.
Up to ¾ oz ordinarily brings a civil fine; a fourth qualifying offence can be criminal. The only New England state without legal sales; a therapeutic programme serves patients.

Adults 21+ have full possession protection for up to 1 oz of licensed cannabis, subject to lawful-source conditions. Over 1–6 oz is decriminalised but excess can be seized. Shops operate; home growing remains criminal.

Public limits are 2 oz of flower, 16 g of extract or 800 mg of edible cannabis. Excess may be stored at home out of public view. Six mature and six immature plants per adult, with twelve mature plants per household. Shops and licensed consumption areas.

2.5 ounces of usable cannabis may be possessed. A person 21 or older may give that amount, or one-fourth of an ounce of concentrate, without payment, if the gift is not advertised or promoted to the public. Home growing is six plants per adult and twelve at a residence, and only more than 25 miles from a licensed adult-use shop unless a medical exception applies. Licensed consumption lounges operate in Las Vegas.
3 oz on you and 5 lb at home. Three mature and three immature plants per adult, and six of each per household. Smoking cannabis is allowed almost anywhere tobacco smoking is.

2.5 oz from a licensed dispensary or home growing, and six plants per adult, twelve per household. A gift of up to 2.5 oz, or 15 g of extract, is lawful only at a private home or farm. Licensed shops since August 2024.

Without a card, possession is a misdemeanour. The medical programme has no list of qualifying conditions. Sharing less than 3 grams of medical marijuana without payment is a $400 administrative fine and is not a criminal prosecution.

Usable marijuana is limited to 2 oz in public and 8 oz per household; extracts have a separate 1 oz limit and licensed-source requirement. Four plants per household. Adult gifts of usable marijuana are limited to 1 oz at a time. Licensed shops since 2015.
30 g or less is a misdemeanour with up to 30 days in jail, cut to a small fine in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and other cities. A large medical programme operates.
1 oz in public and 10 oz at home; three mature and three immature plants per dwelling. More than 1 oz through 2 oz is a $150 civil penalty. Licensed shops since December 2022.
First possession of 1 oz or less can bring 30 days in jail. Above 1 oz can support a felony intent-to-distribute charge; simple possession remains a misdemeanour. No medical programme.
Up to 2 oz is a misdemeanour with up to a year in jail, and ingesting cannabis is itself an offence. Medical cannabis is available to card holders.
½ oz or less is a misdemeanour with up to a year in jail. Only low-THC oil is permitted for a few conditions.
2 oz or less is a misdemeanour with up to 180 days in jail; several cities no longer enforce it. A restricted low-THC medical programme was widened in 2025.
Under 1 oz is a misdemeanour with up to six months in jail. Medical cannabis is sold through licensed pharmacies; smoking it is not allowed.

Possession and four plants per household have been legal since 2021. After years of vetoes, a retail law was enacted in 2026; adult-use sales are scheduled for 1 July 2027. Until then medical dispensaries are the only legal place to buy.

A person 21 or older may possess up to 2 oz, or 10 g of hashish, and two mature plus four immature plants. A gift of up to 1 oz, or 5 g of hashish, between adults is legal if it is not advertised. The first state to legalise through its legislature; shops since 2022. Specified prior drug-selling convictions trigger stricter possession and plant rules.

1 ounce of useable cannabis is legal for a person 21 or older, and shops have operated since 2014. A qualifying patient may grow at home, including four plants with a valid authorization and no entry in the medical database. Growing outside that permission is a class C felony.

Without a qualifying prior drug conviction, THC possession carries up to six months. An earlier drug conviction can make even a first cannabis case a felony. No medical programme; local penalties vary.

Possession carries 90 days to six months and/or a fine. First possession under 15 g must follow the conditional-discharge procedure; dismissal requires successful probation. Medical dispensaries serve card holders.

Unauthorised possession is criminal: the first-offence misdemeanour ceilings are 3 oz of plant material, 0.3 g of liquid, or 3 g of powder or pills. Larger amounts can bring a felony. No medical programme.
First country to legalise (2013). Registered residents choose between growing six plants, joining a club, or buying up to 40 g a month in pharmacies at state-set prices.

Small personal cannabis holdings can bring a fine or up to fifteen days of administrative detention; above 1 g of dried cannabis they become criminal, with up to three years in prison for the basic offence. Growing and supplying cannabis are criminal, and since June 2026 public use is an administrative offence. Industrial hemp is licensed at 0.2% THC; medical cannabis has no patient route.
Up to 2 oz is decriminalised and a licensed medical industry, including traditional growers, operates since 2018.

Personal-use cases are dealt with through court-ordered rehabilitation. Separate criminal possession can bring one to two years even within the twenty-gram cannabis band. Growing no more than ten plants carries six to ten years in prison.

Cannabis possession, supply, cultivation and use are offences. The House passed medical-licensing and record-clearing bills in 2020, but an official July 2026 review still reported both awaiting assent. In 2023 the premier proposed a route for doctors under existing legislation.

The Cannabis Use Act sets adult possession limits at two ounces. Qualified resident patients may grow six flowering and six immature plants. By September 2026 the first commercial grow had approval to operate and the testing lab was operational; an October update still reported no dispensary sales.

A first detection of use brings administrative monitoring; repeat detection can lead to addiction assessment. Criminal use penalties depend on specified rehabilitation-related statuses. Illegal sale carries three to seven years, rising to life or death in the highest cannabis weight bands.

Cannabis possession, supply and unlicensed growing are crimes. Court guidance distinguishes small personal grows from commercial cultivation. Medical-cannabis licences authorise production for export, while adult-use sales remain prohibited.
Possession, use and supply carry up to 14 years; a 2017 recommendation to regulate medicinal use was not adopted. There is no medical, hemp or CBD exemption.

Cannabis use brings three days’ administrative arrest; possession and growing carry prison terms. The highest supply tiers allow life or death on paper, but the death penalty has been under a moratorium since 1993 and was barred in peacetime by the 2007 law; no cannabis execution or cannabis-specific death sentence was found.
Possession is criminal. A first offence with less than three grams can bring a fine or up to one year in prison.

Cannabis possession and use remain criminal offences, but eligible people can accept supervised treatment before sentence. Successful completion avoids a sentence and a conviction entry. Growing and supply are excluded from that route, and people who breach its conditions can return to sentencing.

Cannabis is controlled through inherited Somali drug laws, with prison terms for unauthorised possession, cultivation and supply. Those laws contain medical licensing provisions. Somaliland police reported a cultivation arrest in Hargeisa in 2023.

Small possession can bring a fine or up to thirty days’ administrative arrest. Large personal possession can carry up to three years in prison. Growing below the criminal threshold brings a warning or fine; large-scale growing and supplying cannabis remain crimes.
Holding or growing cannabis for personal use carries five years in prison, with residential treatment possible instead. Unpaid supply can bring death or twenty-five years.

A 2018 Constitutional Court ruling protects adult possession, use and cultivation in private, and the 2024 Cannabis for Private Purposes Act writes that into law. The Act is not yet in force: draft regulations published in February 2026 propose caps of 750 g and five plants. Buying and selling remain illegal.

The Cannabis Act of 2021 would license medicinal growing, but it has not come into force. Industrial hemp has been under licence since 3 January 2025. Possession without lawful authority remains a serious offence.

Recreational cannabis remains criminalised. The criminal code provides a fine, up to five years in prison, or both for unlawful possession, use or personal cultivation. Medical production and industrial hemp have separate licensing routes.
